# Avoid False Incentives

> "But seek first God's Kingdom and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well."
>
> — Matthew 6:33

Men on the Willpower Method are always short of motivation, so they manufacture some. They bolt a prize onto the end of quitting and hope the prize will drag them through.

The plainest version is the bribe: "If I get to the end of the month, I'll buy myself those trainers." It sounds sensible. But be honest. Would any man in the trap swap his nightly comfort for a pair of shoes? One experienced Christian counsellor, who has helped a great many men and deserves respect for it, builds a whole system this way: a holiday in Greece for a clean year, and for a fall, a penalty such as eating a raw onion. The trouble is the same in both directions. The bribe only tells him that the month ahead is something to be endured, and that what he's leaving behind was worth compensating him for. The sacrifice has just got bigger in his mind.

The internet has built grander prizes than trainers. Here are the four you're most likely to meet.

## 1. The superpowers {-}

Spend an evening on the NoFap forums and you'll be promised a great deal: a deeper voice, clear skin, an "aura", and women drawn across the room by forces unknown. One of the coaches this book quotes gladly on other things goes all the way here: "And this is literally proven, right? If you do NOFAP, you're going to be attractive." He even credits it for the glow on his face.

It isn't proven. A therapist who works with these men said of the whole list, "there is little medical evidence for any of these changes." Chapter 4 called this the opposite lie, and it does its damage right here. You stop. Day twelve arrives. You inspect the mirror and find the same face. No aura. The barista hasn't noticed a thing. Now a voice says, "It isn't working. You gave it up for nothing." You were promised wages, the wages didn't come, and you go back to the old job.

The honest men in that world say so themselves. One popular teacher of retention put out a video called "Women Can Smell the Retention on You", and then admitted on camera: "a lot of these ideas I hate the fact that they can't be backed up more scientifically". A man on the NoFap forum reported back after a full year, having hoped among other things for his hair: "I expected my lost hair to regrow, but instead it receded even more, so this expectation is broken." Another, ninety days free, said the wisest thing on the whole subject: "the so-called non-fap 'superpower benefits' are just qualities we would have if we weren't pmo addicts". They aren't powers. They're what a man is like when nothing is draining him.

Even the bluntest coach quoted in this book, who is no friend of the habit, laughs at the magic. A caller told him he was two years into retention. The coach told him he was hoping for "some Magic", and that the real reason was that he was scared of girls. A psychiatrist who has looked at the claims says of them, "we don't really know if it's true". Then he makes the sensible case, which is the one this book makes: "if you look at the harms of pornography addiction and then you start doing nofap and you free yourself of that physiologic cycle that can be a net positive".

## 2. "I'll quit to get women" {-}

A close cousin. The pitch is that the energy you save becomes the fuel that gets you the girl. In the same coach's words, that energy "is what's going to drive you to get the woman you want".

The retention teacher takes it further. He advises men to train in a gym full of attractive women and turn the tension into fuel. And even he sets a limit on the promise: "I don't think being on retention will create desire from women who aren't already interested in you".

Look at what this does. It leaves lust exactly where it was and just points it somewhere else. Jesus didn't say to harness the look. He said the look was already the sin. You're still treating women as the prize and your own desire as the boss. And it sets a trap with two doors. Suppose you don't get the girl. Then you're miserable, quitting "failed", and you know where you go for comfort. Suppose you do get her. Then the incentive has been paid out and there's nothing left holding you. Either way you're back.

The Christian version is a bargain with God: "Lord, I'll give this up, and You'll send me a wife." God isn't a vending machine, and He's not fooled about who that deal is for.

## 3. The 90-day badge {-}

Chapter 10 dealt with the counter. The badge is the counter with a finish line. NoFap's own guide describes ninety days as a challenge, and to be fair it adds a warning of its own: "rebooting is not a linear process!"

A challenge is a thing you get through. It makes the days into a sentence to be served, with freedom scheduled for day ninety-one. And what happens on day ninety-one? The badge is won, the reason has expired, and the Big Monster hasn't been touched. Plenty of men "celebrate". Do you want to stop for ninety days, or do you want to be free?

The group version is the pact: six men in a chat, all starting on Monday. It fails for three reasons. First, you can't make another man ready, and pressure only makes the habit more precious, so the unready ones carry on in secret. Second, everyone is leaning on everyone else, waiting it out together like men doing penance. When one falls, the rest have the excuse they were hoping for. "I'd have made it, but Dave cracked." (Most of them had cracked already.) Third, even the glory gets split six ways.

Don't confuse a pact with honesty. Chapter 15 told you to bring this into the light, and it meant it. Telling a trusted brother the truth is good for you. Making your freedom depend on his streak is not.

## 4. "I'll quit once I'm married" {-}

This one is an incentive in reverse. It doesn't promise a prize for stopping. It promises that marriage will do the stopping for you, so you needn't bother yet.

Ask the married men. On one coach's livestream a 57-year-old caller says, "I've been married for 27 years", and then admits he was looking at porn as recently as six months ago. Even Dr Dobson, who took the soft line you met in Chapter 4, listed carrying the habit into marriage among his worries.

A wedding doesn't kill either monster. The Little Monster doesn't want a wife. He wants his routine, at his hour, with nobody else to consider. You'd simply be carrying the trap over the threshold, and now it hurts two people. The time to be a man your wife can trust is before you meet her.

## Why none of them work {-}

Every one of these makes the same mistake. It ties stopping to a payment. If the payment doesn't arrive, you feel cheated. If it does arrive, the novelty wears off and you feel deprived. In both cases you start asking, "Is this really making my life better? Did I do it wrong?" Doubt like that is what urges are made of.

Stop kidding yourself. The real costs are enormous: years of evenings, a foggy head, a conscience you can't look at, a word you can't keep. If those haven't stopped you, a badge and a pair of trainers won't. All a phoney prize can do is make the sacrifice look bigger.

So look at the other end of the rope and ask the questions from Chapter 1. What is it doing for me? NOTHING. Why do I need it? YOU DON'T. YOU'RE ONLY PUNISHING YOURSELF.

Will good things follow? Almost certainly. Men report more energy, more nerve and clearer heads, and you'll hear from them in a couple of chapters. But those are a bonus. Jesus put it in the right order in the verse above: seek the Kingdom first, and the other things get added. Seek the other things first and you get neither. A man may well stop this and be single, spotty and broke a year later. He'll still be free, and he still won't miss it.

One last thing. Don't announce your quitting to the world, or post "Day 1" anywhere. Nobody else much cares. An announcement turns you into a proud ex-addict with an audience to perform for. What you want to be is a happy man who simply doesn't do it. (Quietly handing this book to a man who needs it is a different thing, and the last chapters come to that.) When the thought of it wanders in, don't shove it away. Notice it, and say: "Thank God, I'm free of that." Then carry on with your day.

A man on the NoFap forum got there after seventy-six days and wrote the sentence this chapter has been aiming at: "I realize I do not need a why anymore."
